title: Ripple marks
sentences: In geology, ripple marks are sedimentary structures (i.e., bedforms of the lower flow regime) and indicate agitation by water (current or waves) or directly by wind.
Current ripple marks, unidirectional ripples, or asymmetrical ripple marks are asymmetrical in profile, with a gentle up-current slope and a steeper down-current slope.
The down-current slope is the angle of repose, which depends on the shape of the sediment.
These commonly form in fluvial and aeolian depositional environments, and are a signifier of the lower part of the Lower Flow Regime.
Ripple cross-laminae forms when deposition takes place during migration of current or wave ripples.
A series of cross-laminae are produced by superimposing migrating ripples.
The ripples form lateral to one another, such that the crests of vertically succeeding laminae are out of phase and appear to be advancing upslope.
This process results in cross-bedded units that have the general appearance of waves in outcrop sections cut normal to the wave crests.
In sections with other orientations, the laminae may appear horizontal or trough-shaped, depending upon the orientation and the shape of the ripples.

Ripple cross-laminae will always have a steeper dip downstream, and will always be perpendicular to paleoflow meaning the orientation of the ripples will be in a direction that is ninety degrees to the direction that current if flowing.
Scientists suggest current drag, or the slowing of current velocity, during deposition is responsible for ripple cross-laminae.
Wave-formed ripples (also called bidirectional ripples, or symmetrical ripple marks) develop where oscillatory water motion generated by surface waves moves sediment across the bed.
They commonly have approximately symmetrical profiles and straight or gently sinuous crests.
Their geometry depends on factors including sediment grain size and the velocity and orbital diameter of the near-bed water motion.
Symmetry is not unique to wave-formed ripples, nor are all wave-formed ripples symmetrical.
Shoaling or breaking waves may produce unequal motion in opposite directions, resulting in asymmetric wave ripples.
Ripples formed by a combination of oscillatory wave motion and a unidirectional current may also have asymmetric or more complex profiles.
Wave-formed ripples are most commonly preserved in sediments deposited in shallow marine, lacustrine, and tidal-flat environments.
Their presence indicates oscillatory near-bed flow, although ripple shape alone may not be sufficient to reconstruct the depositional environment.
Aeolian ripples are small bedforms produced when wind transports loose sediment by saltation and surface creep.
Their crests lie approximately transverse to the direction of net sediment transport.
Impact ripples are the most common small aeolian ripples.
They develop through interactions between saltating grains and grains resting or moving along the surface.
Repeated impacts preferentially move grains from troughs towards crests, causing the ripple pattern to migrate downwind.
In sediment containing grains of different sizes, coarser grains may become concentrated near the ripple crests.
Aeolian megaripples are larger bedforms, intermediate in scale between ordinary impact ripples and dunes.
On Earth, their wavelengths range from several tens of centimetres to several metres.
They typically develop in poorly sorted or bimodal sediment, where saltating finer grains cause coarser grains to move by shorter hops or surface creep.
The coarser fraction may form an armoured layer, particularly near the crests.
Also known as aerodynamic ripples, these are formed with fine, well-sorted grain particles accompanied by high velocity winds which result in long, flat ripples.
The flat ripples are formed by long saltation paths taken by grains in suspension and grains on the ground surface.

The opposite of a crest, so the minimum value or height in a wave.
It is the location at the very lowest point of a wave cycle also shown in picture to right.
The lee side has a steeper slope than the stoss.
The lee is always on the back side of the ripple, which is also on the opposite side of where the current flow meets the ripple.
The current flows down the lee side.
The stoss is the side of a wave or ripple that has a gentle slope versus a steeper slope.
Current always flows up the stoss side and down the lee side.
This can be used to determine current flow during the time of ripple formation.
